newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori popularity soars, Japanese envoy arrives.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori popularity soars, Japanese envoy arrives.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori's popularity has soared after a successful raid on the besieged Japanese ambassador's house, an opinion poll showed, as details emerged of the hostages' miserable life in captivity.

A survey by polling agency Apoyo SA conducted the day after the raid and released late on Wednesday showed Fujimori's popularity shot up to 67 percent from 38 percent four days ago, Apoyo director Alfredo Torres said.

The poll of 420 people in metropolitan Lima, where about one-third of Peruvians live, showed 84 percent approved of the assault on the residence, in which elite commandos rescued all but one of the 72 hostages alive. Only 10 percent disapproved.
Two soldiers and all 14 of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas died in the 40-minute gunbattle.
But even some of Fujimori's supporters expected the euphoria and worldwide praise for the raid to fade soon, saying he still faced a litany of problems in this poor, crisis-ridden country.

"Every government has its ups and downs. I wouldn't expect this rise in its popularity to last long, certainly not two or three years," said congressman Carlos Ferrero of Fujimori's Cambio '90-New Majority party.
The raid gave Peru's military one of the biggest victories ever in its fratricidal, 17-year-long war with leftist rebels, in which about 30,000 people have died.
"There is clearly support -- whether it lasts or not -- for how the president has dealt with the conflict," said Apoyo's Torres on local television.

Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda arrived in Lima early on Thursday in time for clean-up operations at the gutted residence, where police were sweeping the grounds for landmines and booby traps.

Fujimori said on Wednesday that no one outside his security forces -- not even the Japanese government -- had advance knowledge of the raid on what is, under international law, sovereign Japanese territory.

But there was no sign of a serious rift in relations with Japan, one of Peru's top aid donors. Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he would not second-guess Fujimori's use of force after months of negotiations led nowhere.

With the bloodied corpses of the Marxist rebels still lying where they died, Fujimori on Wednesday toured the gutted mansion the morning after the raid. Peruvian television showed grisly images of him inspecting the house and stepping gingerly past the body of MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini -- a bullet hole in his head and a gash across his neck.
At least two other bodies lay next to Cerpa, bloodied,
mangled and lying on a grand staircase leading to the main reception hall.

The interior of the house appeared destroyed as Fujimori walked through its once elegant rooms. A gaping hole in the floor showed where troops swarmed in Tuesday afternoon to free the captives held by guerrillas for 126 days.
The few hostages willing to talk publicly during their first full day of freedom spoke of a depressing life under MRTA guns, coping with rats, cold food and bullying rebels.

One hostage said the rebels continually ran the 72 captives through drills in case of assault. The drills would end with the guerrillas pointing their weapons at captives bunched into small groups and threatening to blow them up.

"They made us believe they were all carrying explosives," said the liberated hostage, congressman Carlos Blanco, adding that MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa "always had an aggressive attitude and the most profound disdain for human life."
One of the most difficult aspects of their long captivity was a lack of sleep in the mouse-infested ambassador's mansion, another hostage said.

"The mice were all over us. This was so ... disgusting, that the number of rodents did not let us sleep," said hostage and Jesuit priest Juan Julio Wicht. "We were very lucky to have been able to keep our mental state in order."

Fujimori on Wednesday gave details of how crack troops carried out the raid, including a warning given to the hostages about 10 minutes before the raid. He did not reveal how they got the warning, but military sources said the hostages got word by way of a beeper carried by retired naval officer Luis Giampetri Rojas, telling them not to panic and keep their heads down.
Giampetri had apparently managed to keep the beeper concealed from the rebel captors during the four-month ordeal.

Minutes later commandos burst into the building through at least four tunnels, where they had laid in wait since Monday, in a blaze of bullets and explosions, catching the guerrillas off-guard as they played soccer on the ground floor.

Dozens of soldiers swept through holes blasted into the walls and through the front door, startling the rebels who tried to flee up the stairs to the second floor but got no farther than the staircase before being gunned down. More commandos took the roof and began hustling away the hostages.
